[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md#core-principles]

### Core Principles

The following principles guide AI infrastructure and platform security architecture at Gainwell, addressing unique ML infrastructure challenges beyond traditional cloud security.
page_texts.10:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md#principle-1-harden-ml-platforms-to-security-baselines]

#### Principle 1: Harden ML Platforms to Security Baselines

**Description**: Configure ML platforms (SageMaker, Azure ML, Databricks) to documented security baselines aligned with vendor best practices and industry standards. Continuously validate compliance and remediate drift.

**Rationale**: Managed ML platforms have dozens of configuration options impacting security (network isolation, IAM, encryption, logging). Default configurations prioritize ease of use over security. Inconsistent configurations across projects create gaps. Security baselines codify required controls; automated validation ensures adherence.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL implement documented security baselines for each ML platform, covering network isolation, IAM least privilege, encryption at rest and in transit, audit logging, and private endpoint requirements
- The capability SHALL define and manage ML infrastructure as code in version-controlled repositories; all infrastructure configuration changes SHALL be applied through code pipelines
- The capability SHALL conduct automated compliance scanning of ML platform configurations against security baselines and SHALL alert on detected deviations; deviations SHALL be remediated within defined SLAs
- The capability SHOULD deploy ML platforms as immutable infrastructure; running infrastructure SHALL be replaced rather than patched for significant changes
- The capability SHALL incorporate updated vendor security guidance and industry benchmarks into ML platform security baselines as guidance evolves

**Reference**: CIS Benchmarks for AWS/Azure/GCP, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-2 (Baseline Configuration), NIST CSF 2.0 "Identify" and "Protect" functions.

---

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md#principle-2-secure-containers-for-ml-workloads]

#### Principle 2: Secure Containers for ML Workloads

**Description**: Build, scan, sign, and monitor ML containers throughout their lifecycle. Enforce container security policies at runtime to prevent exploitation and breakouts.

**Rationale**: Containers are the primary deployment mechanism for ML workloads. Vulnerable or misconfigured containers are common attack vectors. ML containers often require elevated privileges for GPU access, increasing risk. Container security requires defense-in-depth: secure builds, vulnerability scanning, runtime protection, and monitoring.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- ML container base images SHALL extend the enterprise-approved base images and hardening standards defined in [STD-APP-CNT-001](../../../../standards/application/container/STD-APP-CNT-001-container-deployment.md) and [STD-TEC-EKS-006](../../../../standards/technology/eks/STD-TEC-EKS-006-security.md); where ML frameworks or GPU drivers require framework-specific base images, those images SHALL still adhere to the hardening requirements in those standards (minimal OS footprint, non-root user, read-only root filesystem) and SHALL be regularly updated and vulnerability-scanned
- The capability SHALL scan all ML container images for vulnerabilities before deployment; images with critical or high CVEs SHALL be blocked from production
- The capability SHALL sign container images with organizational keys and SHALL verify image signatures before deployment
- The capability SHALL enforce runtime security policies that limit container capabilities; privileged container execution SHALL be prevented where not technically required for GPU access
- The capability SHALL deploy runtime security monitoring for ML containers to detect anomalous process execution, unexpected network connections, and unauthorized file-system access

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-190 (Application Container Security), CIS Docker Benchmark, CIS Kubernetes Benchmark, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-7 (Software Integrity).

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md#principle-3-enforce-least-privilege-for-mlops-access]

#### Principle 3: Enforce Least Privilege for MLOps Access

**Description**: Grant minimal IAM permissions necessary for ML workflows. Implement role-based access control (RBAC) with fine-grained permissions per team, project, and environment. Regularly review and revoke excessive access.

**Rationale**: Overprivileged credentials are high-value targets. ML platforms require permissions to compute, storage, and services; poorly scoped permissions enable privilege escalation, data exfiltration, or resource abuse. Least privilege reduces blast radius of credential compromise.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL define per-persona IAM roles for ML workflows (data scientist, ML engineer, MLOps engineer, security engineer) with minimal permissions; wildcard or full-platform role assignments SHALL be prohibited
- The capability SHALL enforce separate IAM roles per environment (development, staging, production), with production roles applying more restrictive permissions and requiring stronger audit controls
- The capability SHALL assign dedicated service accounts or IAM roles per ML project, scoped to project-specific resources only; cross-project credential sharing SHALL be prohibited
- The capability SHOULD support just-in-time temporary credential elevation for administrative MLOps tasks, with access automatically revoked after a defined time window
- The capability SHALL conduct automated quarterly reviews of MLOps IAM permissions and SHALL revoke unused or excessive permissions

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-6 (Least Privilege), NIST Zero Trust Architecture (NIST SP 800-207), CIS AWS/Azure IAM Benchmarks.

---

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md#principle-4-isolate-gpu-resources-and-monitor-for-abuse]

#### Principle 4: Isolate GPU Resources and Monitor for Abuse

**Description**: Implement multi-tenancy controls for GPU compute ensuring teams cannot access or exhaust each other's resources. Monitor GPU usage for anomalies indicating crypto-mining or abuse.

**Rationale**: GPU compute is expensive ($3-5/hour per A100 GPU) and scarce. Shared GPU resources without isolation enable noisy neighbors, budget overruns, and resource starvation. Adversaries hijack GPU instances for crypto-mining when credentials compromised. Isolation and monitoring are essential for GPU governance.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL enforce per-team and per-project GPU resource quotas to prevent resource exhaustion and noisy-neighbor effects in shared ML compute environments
- The capability SHALL dedicate Kubernetes namespaces to teams with RBAC preventing cross-namespace GPU resource access and network policies isolating namespace traffic
- When shared GPU compute platforms are in use, hardware partitioning mechanisms (such as NVIDIA MIG or equivalent) SHALL be enforced to provide secure isolation between workloads; GPU partitions SHALL be assigned per-project or per-team to prevent cross-tenant GPU memory access
- The capability SHALL monitor GPU utilization, running processes, and workload characteristics against established normal baselines
- The capability SHALL detect and alert on anomalous GPU usage patterns consistent with unauthorized workloads such as cryptocurrency mining

**Reference**: NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) documentation, Kubernetes Resource Quotas, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-6 (Resource Availability).

---

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md#principle-5-segment-ml-networks-and-control-egress]

#### Principle 5: Segment ML Networks and Control Egress

**Description**: Deploy ML workloads in dedicated network segments with least-privilege network access. Control egress traffic to prevent data exfiltration and command-and-control (C2) communication.

**Rationale**: Flat networks allow compromised ML workloads to access databases, enterprise applications, or other ML projects inappropriately. Unrestricted egress enables data exfiltration and C2 communication. Network segmentation limits lateral movement; egress controls reduce exfiltration risk. While dedicated VPCs provide the strongest isolation posture, no industry standard mandates VPC-level isolation specifically for AI workloads — NIST SP 800-53 SC-7 governs boundary protection generally, and NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture) emphasizes identity-based controls over perimeter-based isolation. Namespace and subnet-level isolation is therefore the mandatory baseline, with dedicated VPCs as a strongly recommended defense-in-depth measure.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- All production AI workloads SHALL be deployed in dedicated Kubernetes namespaces or subnets with enforced network policies restricting pod-to-pod and pod-to-external communication
- Deploying AI workloads in VPCs dedicated to AI/ML use cases, isolated from general enterprise application VPCs, SHOULD be implemented as a defense-in-depth measure; this is especially recommended for AI systems in the High-risk tier per [GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06 §AI System Risk Classification](GUID-SEC-AI-GOV-2.9.06.MD)
- Separate subnets SHALL be used for training environments (no inbound internet), inference environments (controlled ingress), and experimentation environments (restricted internet access)
- The capability SHALL enforce private endpoint connectivity for ML platform access in production and PHI-processing environments; public endpoints for production inference and training platforms SHALL be disabled
- ML workload egress SHALL be routed through proxies or NAT gateways with destination allowlists; egress attempts SHALL be logged and alerts SHALL fire on access to unauthorized destinations
- Network policies SHALL restrict pod-to-pod communication to explicitly authorized service interactions only

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SC-7 (Boundary Protection), AWS VPC Security Best Practices, Azure Virtual Network Security, NIST Zero Trust Architecture.

---

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md#principle-6-centralize-secrets-management-for-ml-workflows]

#### Principle 6: Centralize Secrets Management for ML Workflows

**Description**: Store all ML credentials (API keys, database passwords, cloud credentials) in centralized secrets management services. Rotate secrets automatically; enforce no hardcoded secrets in code or notebooks.

**Rationale**: Hardcoded secrets in notebooks, training scripts, or Git repos are frequently exposed. Manual secret management is error-prone. Centralized secrets management provides controlled access, audit trails, automatic rotation, and encryption. Gainwell's enterprise approach to secrets management is established in [ADR-SEC-002 — Centralized Secrets Strategy](../../../../decisions/security/ADR-SEC-002-centralized-secrets-strategy.md); AI/ML workloads SHALL comply with that ADR.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- All ML credentials SHALL be stored in enterprise-approved secrets management services per [ADR-SEC-002 — Centralized Secrets Strategy](../../../../decisions/security/ADR-SEC-002-centralized-secrets-strategy.md)
- Secrets SHALL be injected at runtime into ML workloads; secrets SHALL NOT be stored in container images, code, or pipeline definitions
- Automatic rotation SHALL be enabled for database credentials and service accounts; ML workflows SHALL be designed to tolerate rotation without downtime
- Git repositories, container images, and notebooks SHALL be scanned for hardcoded secrets in CI/CD pipelines; commits or images containing secrets SHALL be blocked
- All secret access SHALL be logged and integrated with the enterprise SIEM per ADR-SEC-002

**Reference**: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 IA-5 (Authenticator Management), CIS Secrets Management Benchmarks, OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet.

---
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/GUID-SEC-AI-INFRA-2.9.03.md#principle-7-secure-mlops-cicd-pipelines]

#### Principle 7: Secure MLOps CI/CD Pipelines

**Description**: Integrate security gates into MLOps CI/CD pipelines: vulnerability scanning, policy validation, artifact signing, and deployment approvals. Maintain audit trails of all deployments.

**Rationale**: CI/CD pipelines for ML lack security controls common in application development. Vulnerable containers, misconfigured infrastructure, or malicious artifacts deploy to production without review. Insecure pipelines enable supply chain attacks. Security gates prevent vulnerabilities from reaching production.

**Capability Characteristics**:

- The capability SHALL integrate container vulnerability scanning, configuration policy validation, and security testing as automated gates in MLOps CI/CD pipelines; the pipeline SHALL block progression on critical security violations
- The capability SHALL sign all ML artifacts (container images, models, datasets) in CI/CD pipelines; artifact signatures SHALL be verified before deployment
- The capability SHALL require documented manual approvals for production ML deployments; the approver identity and approval rationale SHALL be recorded in the audit trail
- The capability SHALL define MLOps pipeline configurations as versioned code; ad-hoc manual pipeline modifications outside the code pipeline SHALL be prohibited
- The capability SHALL log all pipeline executions with sufficient context to establish a complete audit trail, including who triggered the pipeline, what was deployed, and the approval status

**Reference**: NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) SP 800-218, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-10 (Developer Configuration Management), CIS Software Supply Chain Security Guide.
